courses.title: Introduction to Computational Thinking
courses.heading: CS 1014: Introduction to Computational Thinking

body.v:
Computational thinking as a perspective rather than a skill — problem formulation, applying computational
tools to large-scale problems across domains, a basic introduction to algorithms and one practical
language, plus the societal and ethical implications of computational systems.

Built for non-majors who want computational literacy without committing to programming. Perfectly
reasonable at what it does. CS majors skip it entirely.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring · Pathways 5F + 10**
**Prerequisites:** none

courses.title: Introduction to Programming in C
courses.heading: CS 1044: Introduction to Programming in C

body.v: Structured programming in C: statement sequencing, logic control, structured data, input/output, functions.

A legacy service course for engineering majors. The 44% would-take-again rate is among the worst in the
department, and it sits alongside a *low* difficulty rating — which says the frustration is with delivery,
not with rigor. CS majors belong in CS 1114, and will learn substantially more C in CS 2505 anyway.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Spring only**
**Prerequisites:** none · partially duplicates CS 1344

courses.title: Introduction to Programming in Java
courses.heading: CS 1054: Introduction to Programming in Java

body.v:
Introductory object-oriented programming in Java: control flow, classes, objects, methods, instantiation,
message passing, plus the impact of computing on diversity and inclusion.

The lowest-rated introductory course at VT. Unlike CS 1044, it is also genuinely hard for what it is — a
4.21 difficulty rating on an intro course is a pacing red flag, and the sub-3.0 GPA backs that up.
Superseded by CS 1114 for majors.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall only · Pathways 5F + 11**
**Prerequisites:** none

courses.title: Introduction to Programming in Python
courses.heading: CS 1064: Introduction to Programming in Python

body.v:
Python fundamentals framed around scientific and engineering problems: control flow, state tracing, simple
and complex types, functional and object-oriented organization, data processing, debugging.

**The best-rated large course in the department**, and it is essentially one professor. **John Lewis**
collects sustained 4–5/5 ratings across dozens of reviews — "best professor I have had at Virginia Tech"
recurs verbatim. Students describe clear explanations, generous deadlines, and consistent accessibility.

Not a CS-major course. But if you are an engineering or science student who needs exactly one programming
course, this is the one, and Lewis is the reason.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · Pathways 5F + 10**
**Prerequisites:** none
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 3/10 for CS majors, 8/10 for everyone else · Teaching A**
courses.usefulness_raw: 3/10 for CS majors, 8/10 for everyone else

courses.title: Introduction to Software Design
courses.heading: CS 1114: Introduction to Software Design

body.v:
Object-oriented programming fundamentals, basic software engineering principles, simple data types, control
structures, arrays and strings, basic algorithms, testing and debugging, and a model of the computer as an
abstract machine.

**The worst student experience of any required course, on every metric available.** Lowest
would-take-again in the core, second-lowest GPA, and a 15.8% withdrawal rate — roughly one student in six
does not finish.
The instructor spread is the story:

A third of students in Edwards' sections withdrew. Recent bright spot: **David McPherson** collects repeated
5/5 ratings through 2026 ("class and projects were easy... he is great").

The dominant complaint across CS 1114 and CS 2114 is **Web-CAT**, VT's automated grader — finicky submission
behavior and steep late penalties appear in review after review. Budget time for submission mechanics, not
just for the code.

courses.heading: CS 1944: Computer Science First Year Seminar

courses.header:
**1 credit · Fall, Summer · REQUIRED**
**Prerequisites:** CS 1114 or CS 2064 or ECE 2514

courses.title: Intermediate Programming in Python
courses.heading: CS 2064: Intermediate Programming in Python

body.v:
Advanced control flow and data processing, data structures, computational techniques, object-oriented
programming, and modern data science pipelines — implementation in data science and production
environments.

Aimed at scientists and engineers. It is an accepted alternative prerequisite into CS 2114, which is its
main structural role. Ratings are mediocre across 30 reviews. CS majors have no reason to be here.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · Pathways 5A + 10**
**Prerequisites:** CS 1064

courses.title: Introduction to Problem Solving in Computer Science
courses.heading: CS 2104: Introduction to Problem Solving in Computer Science

body.v:
A broad range of heuristics for solving problems relevant to computation: classical math and word problems,
generating solutions to real-life professional problems, and problem solving through computation.

Genuinely divisive, and the split is instructor-shaped. **Patrick Sullivan** and **Sehrish Nizamani** draw
strong recent reviews — "one of the best CS professors I've ever had," "very helpful and very clearly cares
about her students." **Margaret Ellis** polarizes within the same semester: one 2026 review calls the class
"completely meaningless" with an "absurd amount of classwork," another calls her "amazing... genuinely cares
a lot about her students."
Low difficulty, easy grade, thin skill transfer either way.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · MAJOR REQUIREMENT**
**Prerequisites:** none stated

courses.title: Software Design and Data Structures
courses.heading: CS 2114: Software Design and Data Structures

body.v:
Programming-intensive exploration of software design: advanced object-oriented design, ethics in computing,
algorithm development and analysis, classic data structures, and a team-based software project.

The real on-ramp to the major. Every section runs identical content and format — as one student put it,
"all profs teach the class with identical format + content, so whoever your prof is shouldn't make a big
diff in your grade." The data mostly agrees, with one exception:

**Mohammed Farghally** is the clear pick and draws consistent 4–5/5 reviews ("nice guy who wants you to
learn, and he's very accessible"). Web-CAT frustration dominates the negative comments again, along with
slow TA grading — one 2026 review describes a grade drifting from an A to a B−/C+ over four weeks as
assignments were marked.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · REQUIRED · Pathways 6D + 10**
**Prerequisites:** CS 1114 or CS 2064
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 9/10 · Teaching C — the content is fine; the autograder experience drags it down**

courses.title: Competitive Problem Solving I
courses.heading: CS 2144: Competitive Problem Solving I

body.v:
Algorithms, data structures, and implementation techniques taught through judged competitive programming.
Arrays, lists, maps, trees; recursion, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, search and traversal, graph
representations, computational geometry; macro and micro optimization.

Formalized out of the old CS 2984 special study (GPA 3.54, n=236 in the sample window). **This is the most
directly interview-shaped course VT offers** — the judged-submission format is LeetCode and ICPC practice,
for credit, with a structure around it.
The enrollment is tiny and self-selecting, so the 3.80 GPA is not a difficulty signal.

courses.header:
**3 credits**
**Prerequisites:** CS 2114
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 6/10 generally, 8/10 if you are grinding technical interviews · Teaching n/d**
courses.usefulness_raw: 6/10 generally, 8/10 if you are grinding technical interviews

courses.title: Foundations of Contemporary Security Environments
courses.heading: CS 2164: Foundations of Contemporary Security Environments

body.v:
Part of the Secure Computing major's foundation. This is a **policy and framing course, not a technical
one** — no exploitation, no cryptographic implementation, no tooling. Useful context, minimal skill
transfer.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** none stated

courses.title: Topics in Programming Systems
courses.heading: CS 2304: Topics in Programming Systems

body.v:
Guided self-study in one specific programming system — JavaScript, C++, CUDA, Ruby, SQL, FORTRAN, UNIX —
covering its syntax and applications.

An underrated way to pick up a concrete, marketable skill for a single credit. The SQL, JavaScript, and CUDA
variants are the ones with real career return.

One caution the numbers make plain: a **7.9% withdrawal rate against a 1.75 difficulty rating**. Nothing
about the material is hard. It is self-paced, and self-paced is where people quietly disappear. Set your own
deadlines in week one.

courses.header:
**1 credit · Fall, Spring · repeatable 3× (max 2× for major credit)**
**Prerequisites:** CS 2114

courses.title: Computer Organization I
courses.heading: CS 2505: Computer Organization I

body.v:
Design and operation of digital computers, working up from the logic gate level: combinational and
sequential circuits, information representation, computer arithmetic, ALUs, control unit design, basic
computer organization, and the relationship between high-level languages and instruction set architectures.
Heavy C programming throughout.

**Allyson Senger** dominates recent reviews and splits sharply. The praise is specific and repeated — caring,
responsive, supportive, "for such a difficult class, she makes it a whole lot easier," "she responds quickly
and makes you feel supported, not judged." The criticism is equally specific: a final exam covering material
barely addressed during the semester. **David McPherson** draws consistent praise for passion and elaboration.
For most students this is the first serious encounter with C and assembly. It is a step change from CS 2114.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · DEGREE CORE**
**Prerequisites:** CS 1114 or CS 2064 (C or better) · corequisite MATH 2534 or MATH 3034
courses.prerequisites: CS 1114 or CS 2064 (C or better) · corequisite MATH 2534 or MATH 3034

courses.title: Computer Organization II
courses.heading: CS 2506: Computer Organization II

body.v:
Instruction formats and construction, addressing modes, instruction execution, **memory hierarchy operation
and performance**, pipelining, input/output, and the relationship between high-level languages and machine
language.

**Second-lowest GPA in the required core**, and since Fall 2025 a hard gate for the capstone. This is where
cache behavior and pipelining stop being trivia and start explaining why your code is slow — the direct
feeder into CS 3214.

**Dimitrios Nikolopoulos** is the interesting case. He runs Discord office hours covering most of the day and
records supplemental lectures, and students single that out as what makes the course survivable — while
simultaneously noting visible frustration in lecture when students don't follow. Reviews of **Senger**'s
final here are unusually bleak.

courses.heading: CS 2964 / 2974 / 2984: Field, Independent, and Special Study

body.v:
Variable-credit vehicles. CS 2984 historically carried "Competitive Problem Solving I" before it became the
standing course CS 2144 — which accounts for most of that 236-student enrollment.
Value depends entirely on the topic and the faculty member involved.

courses.header: **1–19 credits, variable**

body.v:
CS 2704 appears in the current catalog as a stub — contact hours listed, no title, no description. It is a
retired course number. Ignore it if you see it referenced anywhere.

courses.title: Data Structures and Algorithms
courses.heading: CS 3114: Data Structures and Algorithms

body.v:
Advanced data structures and performance analysis: sorting, searching, hashing, advanced tree structures and
algorithms, file system organization and access methods, plus ethical issues in data analysis and software
performance. Projects demand real design and implementation work.

Interview currency, prerequisite for nearly every worthwhile elective, and since Fall 2025 a capstone gate.
Note that despite carrying Pathways 5A it **cannot double-count** with any other requirement — the only
course in the degree with that restriction.

A 1.10 GPA spread across sections of the same required course. **Mohammed Farghally** draws the best recent
reviews — "by far the best professor I've had at VT... good lecturer and gives a lot of leeway." **Yang Cao**
draws the worst: a Spring 2025 review reports a section starting at 150 students and dropping to 40 before
the drop deadline. **Patrick Sullivan** is genuinely split — praised for being approachable and giving clear
answers, criticized in the same term for leaving a midterm ungraded for six weeks.

The standing student advice for the projects: start early, choose your partner carefully, go to office hours
the moment you're stuck.

courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 10/10 · Teaching C+ · The section matters more here than anywhere else in the degree**

courses.title: Computer Systems
courses.heading: CS 3214: Computer Systems

body.v:
Computer systems as they matter to application programmers, with emphasis on operating system principles:
processes, threads, synchronization, deadlock, CPU scheduling, system call interfaces, system-level I/O and
file management, shell programming, separate compilation, loading and linking, IPC, virtual and physical
memory management, garbage collection, and network programming.

**The highest-value course in the catalog.** Four large C projects — shell, malloc, threadpool, web server —
plus exercises. Students report 20+ hours a week for an A and a midterm average around 40%.

The number that matters most is the withdrawal rate: **4.4%, in the hardest course in the major.** People
finish this course. That is what a well-built hard course looks like — real autograders, a maintained public
course site, genuinely scaffolded projects.
Grades are remarkably consistent across instructors — this is run as one course, not six.

**Dan Williams** gets the strongest recent reviews: "an incredible professor... made all the lecture material
clear," "he was nice, knowledgeable, and wanted us to succeed." **Godmar Back** designed the course and
polarizes hard — one 2026 review praises him for teaching in a way that makes you "learn the material well,"
another from the same academic year calls his lectures unfollowable: "he is flying through a Linux terminal
typing at 100 wpm and you can barely follow along."

Worth knowing regardless of your section: multiple students in *other* instructors' sections report studying
exclusively from Back's recorded lectures and finishing ~20 points above the class average.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring · DEGREE CORE**
**Prerequisites:** CS 2506 and CS 3114
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 10/10 · Teaching B+ · If you take one hard course seriously, make it this one**

courses.title: Software Reverse Engineering
courses.heading: CS 3274: Software Reverse Engineering

body.v:
Theory and practice of software reverse engineering: static and dynamic analysis techniques and tools,
reverse engineering of malware and obfuscated binaries, communications and command-and-control analysis,
and reverse engineering of non-binary software.

**The highest withdrawal rate of any CS course in the dataset** — nearly one student in five. Excellent,
genuinely differentiated preparation for security work, and a bad idea if security is not your direction.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Spring only**
**Prerequisites:** (CS 2114 and CS 2506) or (ECE 2534 and ECE 3514)
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 7/10 for security careers, 3/10 otherwise · Teaching n/d**

courses.title: Comparative Languages
courses.heading: CS 3304: Comparative Languages

body.v:
Programming language constructs with emphasis on run-time behavior, studied two ways: the fundamental
elements of languages and their inclusion in commercial systems, and the differences between implementations
of common elements across languages.

The content genuinely broadens how you think about languages. The execution draws fire, and the criticism
appears even inside the positive reviews: exams reward memorizing the syntax of languages you will never use
again.

**David McPherson** is excellent here — "absolutely amazing professor, great at teaching the material and has
very engaging lectures," with the syntax-memorization exams named as the one downside. **Denis Gracanin**
holds the highest GPA in the course *and* the worst reviews in the department: "by far the most dysfunctional
class I have ever taken at Virginia Tech."

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer · MAJOR REQUIREMENT**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 (C or better)

courses.title: Programming Language Theory and Practice
courses.heading: CS 3314: Programming Language Theory and Practice

body.v:
Theoretical basis of programming languages: formal languages, computability theory, type theory, language
design, standard syntax notation, control flow and data representation features, implementation strategies,
and unsolvable problems in the context of programming languages.

A newer course with encouraging early ratings — 4.20 quality against a 2.60 difficulty is a strong opening
combination. Functionally a gentler, more practical blend of CS 3304 and CS 4114 material. If the ideas in
3304 appealed to you but the exams did not, look here.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall only**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114

courses.title: Numerical Methods
courses.heading: CS 3414: Numerical Methods

body.v:
Computational methods for numerical solution of non-linear equations and differential equations,
approximations, iterations, and least squares.

Hard relative to its enrollment size, and narrow in application. Worth taking if you are heading into
scientific computing, simulation, or graduate engineering; otherwise there are better uses of the slot.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** an intro programming course, plus multivariable calculus / differential equations · mutually exclusive with MATH 4404
courses.prerequisites: an intro programming course, plus multivariable calculus / differential equations · mutually exclusive with MATH 4404

courses.title: Professionalism in Computing
courses.heading: CS 3604: Professionalism in Computing

body.v:
Ethical, social, and professional concerns of the computing field: social impact of computing, effects on
society, the responsibilities of computing professionals, case studies, and an overview of computing history.

**The most honest paradox in the catalog.** Perfect instructor ratings, a 3.79 GPA, a 1.11 difficulty rating
— and students say the quiet part out loud: *"Class was extremely easy — probably spent 15 total hours on the
class and got an A... Don't take Prof Dunlap if you want to learn something."*

**Daniel Dunlap** is genuinely well-liked — chill, engaging, forgiving on late work, visibly invested in his
students. The course is reading quizzes, discussion posts, essays, and a partnered case-study presentation.
Take him, take the three credits, and don't expect the course to change you.

courses.header:

courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 2/10 · Teaching A as an experience, F as skill-building**

courses.title: CS Foundations for Computational Modeling & Data Analytics
courses.heading: CS 3634: CS Foundations for Computational Modeling & Data Analytics

body.v: No CS-major grade data.

Survey of the CS concepts and tools that enable computational science and data analytics: data structure
design and implementation, performance analysis, high-performance architectures, parallel computation, and
the operating system concepts that affect large-scale analytics performance.

**Built for CMDA majors, not CS majors.** It is a compressed substitute for CS 3114 and CS 3214 material.
As a CS major you take the real courses instead.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog — CMDA-track

courses.title: Introductory Data Analytics and Visualization
courses.heading: CS 3654: Introductory Data Analytics and Visualization

body.v:
Basic principles and techniques in data analytics: collecting, storing, accessing, and manipulating
standard-size and large datasets; data visualization; and identifying sources of bias.

Light and well-liked. Its main structural role is as the prerequisite for CS 4654. As a CS major you will
find it shallow, but it is the cheapest legitimate entry point into the data track.

courses.prerequisites: an intro programming course, MATH 2204-level calculus, and a statistics course

courses.title: Intermediate Software Design and Engineering
courses.heading: CS 3704: Intermediate Software Design and Engineering

body.v:
Software design principles with emphasis on engineering practice: lifecycle activities including design,
coding, testing, debugging, and maintenance, and how design affects each; peer review, design for reuse,
CASE tools, writing software to specification. Built around a semester-long team project.

The honest student summary: *"This class is a huge group project where you work on an overarching website or
app. You are not taught ANY code. The lectures cover development processes and topics like unit testing."*
That is a fair complaint, and also a fair description of professional software engineering.

Grading is uniformly generous. **Saad Nizamani** draws strong recent reviews — "fair, great attitude, and
always ready to help" — with the pointed caveat that "not all CS professors for this class are this nice."
Avoid **Gracanin** and **Balci** sections.

**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 (C or better) · prerequisite for CS 4704
courses.prerequisites: CS 3114 (C or better) · prerequisite for CS 4704

courses.title: Mobile Software Development
courses.heading: CS 3714: Mobile Software Development

body.v:
The content is reasonable. The delivery is the problem. **Osman Balci** teaches most sections and has six
consecutive 1/5 ratings running through 2026 — "worst professor in the vt cs department in my opinion, his
lectures are so out of date and his office hours were never helpful," alongside repeated accounts of students
being ridiculed for asking questions. The dissenting reviews describe him as blunt and strict but
knowledgeable.
**Esakia** 3.72 GPA versus Balci 3.33 in the same course.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 or equivalent
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 5/10 · Teaching D+ · Only worth it with Esakia or a new instructor**

courses.title: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction
courses.heading: CS 3724: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction

body.v:
Survey of HCI concepts, theory, and practice: the basic components of human-computer interaction and its
interdisciplinary underpinnings; critical evaluation of computer-based technology from a user-oriented rather
than system-oriented perspective, across both human (cognitive, social) and technological (I/O, interaction
styles, devices) thrusts; design guidelines, evaluation methods, participatory design.

Easy, well-liked, and the gateway to an entire branch of the catalog. **D. Scott McCrickard** posts a 3.91
GPA with 0% withdrawals across 175 students. **Amun Kharel** collects repeated 5/5 reviews — "always has
engaging lectures and is passionate about what he teaches," "a very reasonable grader, flexible with
extensions."

**Andrew Kulak** is the weak point in the ratings, though even a defender's review concedes only that he
"grades kind of tough and can come off as a little arrogant" while finding the class interesting.

courses.title: Introduction to GUI Programming and Graphics
courses.heading: CS 3744: Introduction to GUI Programming and Graphics

body.v:
Design and implementation of object-oriented graphical user interfaces and 2D graphics systems: callbacks,
handlers, event listeners, design patterns, layout managers, architectural models; and the mathematical
foundations of graphics — clipping, scan conversion, affine and convex linear transformations, projections,
viewing, structuring.

**The lowest course-level rating in the department at n≥5.** The graphics-math half is legitimate; the GUI
half is dated desktop-toolkit material that transfers poorly to modern frontend work.
If you want graphics, take CS 4204. If you want interface work, take CS 3724.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 and MATH 2114

courses.title: Cloud Software Development
courses.heading: CS 3754: Cloud Software Development

body.v:
Fundamentals of cloud software development: design patterns, APIs, and underlying middleware; developing
distributed multi-tiered enterprise applications that run on a server and are accessed through a web browser
from desktop, laptop, tablet, or phone.

The topic is squarely relevant to modern backend work. The delivery, again under **Balci**, is not: *"his
content is outdated anyways, it's a mostly worthless class. You'll probably get an A but gain little."*
Another review calls the workload atrocious with vague specifications; a third describes him dropping all
deadlines mid-semester "to test our maturity."
**Esakia** posts 3.68 GPA with 4% withdrawals against Balci's 3.34 and 12%.

courses.header:

courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 6/10 with the right instructor, 3/10 otherwise · Teaching D+**

courses.title: Foundations and Applications of Artificial Intelligence
courses.heading: CS 3804: Foundations and Applications of Artificial Intelligence

body.v:
Application-driven introduction to modern AI and ML: a functional view of supervised, unsupervised,
semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning, including generative and large language model capabilities;
using established libraries and cloud-based AI services to build end-to-end applications in vision and
other areas.

The applied, library-first AI course — deliberately shallow on the mathematics. Early ratings are strong and
the difficulty is low.

**Take this instead of CS 4824 only if AI is a tool for you rather than a career.** If you want to work in
ML, CS 4824 is the one that carries weight.

courses.header: **1–19 credits, variable**

courses.title: Data and Algorithm Analysis
courses.heading: CS 4104: Data and Algorithm Analysis

body.v:
Data structures and algorithms from an analytical perspective: theoretical analysis of efficiency, comparing
algorithms on space and run-time, analytical methods for theoretical and practical performance bounds, and
constraints affecting problem solvability.

**The most useful theory elective and the worst-reviewed course in the department.** The subject matter is
what employers mean when they say "algorithms," and it is the natural continuation of CS 3114.

The teaching is the problem, and the reviews name names. **Adrian Sandu** drew three separate one-star
reviews in early 2026 — reads slides in monotone, never works an example problem, has "not ONCE solved a word
problem (the kinds of problems on tests and homeworks)." **T.M. Murali** drew 2024 reviews alleging he
ridiculed and humiliated students in class.

Note that the grades are *fine*. This is the clearest case in the dataset of GPA completely failing to
capture the experience — the five RMP ratings all describe the same two instructors, so treat the 1.00 as a
verdict on specific sections, not on the subject.

courses.title: Introduction to Formal Languages and Automata Theory
courses.heading: CS 4114: Introduction to Formal Languages and Automata Theory

body.v:
Formal languages and the correspondence between language classes and the automata that recognize them:
formal definitions of grammars and acceptors, deterministic and nondeterministic systems, grammar ambiguity,
finite state and pushdown automata, and normal forms.

**The path of least resistance for the theory requirement.** A 0.3% withdrawal rate across 299 students is
essentially nobody. Modest direct career value, but solid grounding if you later take compilers.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring · THEORY ELECTIVE**
**Prerequisites:** MATH 3134 or MATH 3034 — note there is **no CS prerequisite**
courses.prerequisites: MATH 3134 or MATH 3034 — note there is **no CS prerequisite**

courses.title: Theory of Computation
courses.heading: CS 4124: Theory of Computation

body.v:
Theoretical analysis of the computational process: abstract programs, classes of computational machines and
their equivalence, recursive function theory, unsolvable problems, Church's thesis, Kleene's theorem, program
equivalence, generability, acceptability, decidability.

**The lowest GPA of any CS course in the dataset**, across three sections. Maximum difficulty, minimum
industry return.
Choose this only if you are heading toward a theory PhD and want the signal on your transcript.

courses.header:
**3 credits · THEORY ELECTIVE**
**Prerequisites:** MATH 3134 or MATH 3034

courses.title: Quantum Computation and Information Processing
courses.heading: CS 4134: Quantum Computation and Information Processing

body.v: No grade or rating data — recently introduced.

Quantum states and phenomena; quantum communication concepts including superdense coding and teleportation;
classical and quantum circuits and gate sets; quantum algorithms compared to classical ones; quantum
computational complexity classes; density operators, measurements, quantum channels; error correction and the
stabilizer formalism.

Intellectually the most interesting theory option and the one with the least near-term payoff. It counts as
your theory elective, which makes it a legitimate choice if the subject genuinely grabs you — the
opportunity cost is CS 4104, not a free slot.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring · THEORY ELECTIVE**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog

courses.title: Introduction to Database Management Systems
courses.heading: CS 4604: Introduction to Database Management Systems

body.v:
**The best usefulness-to-pain ratio in the entire catalog.** SQL, relational modeling, normalization,
indexing, and transactions — skills you will use in your first week at almost any software job — taught by
instructors students rate perfectly. A 0.6% withdrawal rate and a perfect 5.00 across nine ratings is a
combination nothing else in the department matches.

**Sally Hamouda** — "hands down the best prof at VT... very lenient grader as well, it takes a royal screwup
to get a bad grade." **Sehrish Nizamani** draws five separate 5/5 reviews across 2025-26, singled out for
teaching SQL properly: "she teaches SQL very clearly and makes sure we understand how to write queries
properly, not just memorize them. She also explains things like data modeling and normalization in a simple
way."

Note the senior-standing requirement — you cannot front-load this one, which is a genuine shame given how
much of the rest of the degree it would make more concrete.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 (C or better), senior standing
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 9/10 · Teaching A · Non-negotiable if you want a software job**

courses.title: Linux Kernel Programming
courses.heading: CS 4224: Linux Kernel Programming

body.v:
Design and internal organization of the Linux kernel: kernel subsystems, boot process, memory management,
process and thread model, scheduling, interrupt and exception handling, the virtual file system and concrete
file systems, block I/O and the I/O scheduler, the network stack, device drivers. You modify existing kernel
code and design, implement, test, and evaluate new kernel modules, with kernel and full-stack debugging
throughout.

**The best-kept secret in the catalog.** Zero withdrawals across the sample window. Nothing else available to
an undergraduate signals systems competence this loudly, and the debugging skills transfer everywhere.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Spring only**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog — CS 3214 expected
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 8/10 for systems and infrastructure, 4/10 otherwise · Teaching A−**

courses.title: Parallel Computation
courses.heading: CS 4234: Parallel Computation

body.v:
Parallel computer architectures, models of parallel computation, interconnection networks, parallel algorithm
development and analysis, programming paradigms and languages for parallel computation, performance
measurement and evaluation.
The natural follow-on to CS 3214, and increasingly relevant given where hardware is heading.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3214 (C or better)

courses.title: Computer Network Architecture and Programming
courses.heading: CS 4254: Computer Network Architecture and Programming

body.v:
Computer network architecture and programming network services: DNS, email and MIME, HTTP, SNMP, multimedia;
wired, wireless, and satellite architectures; the OSI model with emphasis on upper layers; congestion
control, quality of service, routing; the Internet protocol suite (IP, TCP, ARP, RARP); server design,
connectionless and concurrent.

Fills the single biggest gap CS 3214 leaves. Low withdrawal, reasonable grades, and directly applicable to
backend and infrastructure work.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog — CS 3214 expected

courses.title: Compiler Design and Implementation
courses.heading: CS 4304: Compiler Design and Implementation

body.v: No recent grade data.

Theory, design, and implementation of a large language translator system: lexical analysis, syntactic
analysis, code generation, and optimization. You build a full translator.

One of the two or three courses that permanently changes how you read code. It does not run every year, so
plan around it rather than assuming availability.

courses.header:
**3 credits · offered sporadically — check the timetable early**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3214 (C or better)

courses.title: Computer Organization III
courses.heading: CS 4504: Computer Organization III

body.v:
Structure, elements, and analysis of modern enterprise computers: performance evaluation of commercial
computing, past and emerging technology trends, the impact of parallelism at multiple levels of architecture,
memory and storage, Amdahl's Law, Flynn's Taxonomy.

The lowest GPA at the 4000 level — but on only 17 students across two sections, so treat that as indicative
rather than settled. Worthwhile if you are heading toward hardware or architecture; largely redundant after
CS 2505, 2506, and 3214 otherwise.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Spring**
**Prerequisites:** ECE 2500 or CS 3214 or ECE 3504 (C or better)
courses.prerequisites: ECE 2500 or CS 3214 or ECE 3504 (C or better)

courses.title: Issues in Scientific Computing
courses.heading: CS 4414: Issues in Scientific Computing

body.v:
Theory and techniques of modern computational mathematics: computing environments, computational linear
algebra, optimization, approximation, parameter identification, finite difference and finite element methods,
symbolic computation. Project-oriented, modeling physical systems with production software.
Highly domain-specific. Five students in the sample window — the numbers mean almost nothing.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** differential equations, MATH 3214, and a programming course
courses.prerequisites: differential equations, MATH 3214, and a programming course

courses.title: Principles of Computer Security
courses.heading: CS 4264: Principles of Computer Security

body.v:
Survey of computer security design principles and models for software systems: cryptographic models and
methods; modern techniques for robust operating systems, software, web applications, large-scale networks,
and data protection; privacy models and techniques; contemporary computer and network security examples.

**No bad option on the instructor bench** — the tightest spread of any elective in the department, which is
itself a signal about how the course is run. High value even if you never work in security; the
threat-modeling instinct transfers to all engineering.

courses.header:
**3 credits**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3214 (C or better) or ECE equivalent · corequisite for CS 4274
courses.prerequisites: CS 3214 (C or better) or ECE equivalent · corequisite for CS 4274

courses.title: Future of Security
courses.heading: CS 4164: Future of Security

body.v:
Identification and analysis of complex real-world security problems and threats to people, organizations, and
nations across domains, roles, and future scenarios: crisis communication, decision-making tools, ethical
principles, and problem-solving methods before, during, and after conflicts, disasters, and attacks. Uses an
experiential learning facility.
Scenario- and policy-oriented rather than technical. Part of the Secure Computing major. Very light.

See also [CS 3274 Software Reverse Engineering](3000-level.md#cs-3274-software-reverse-engineering) — the
most technically demanding security course available, and the highest withdrawal rate in the dataset.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog

courses.title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
courses.heading: CS 4804: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence

body.v:
Problem solving, game playing, and computer vision: search trees and graphs, game trees, block world vision,
syntactic pattern recognition, object matching, natural language, robotics.

Classical AI. The catalog description reads dated, but search, adversarial search, and constraint reasoning
are durable material. **Tu Vu**, formerly of DeepMind, draws a strong 2026 review: "extremely knowledgeable
about all things AI/LLM and gives great lectures... prioritizes learning over assignments."

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 (C or better), senior standing

courses.title: Machine Learning
courses.heading: CS 4824: Machine Learning

body.v:
Algorithms and principles of machine learning, focused on perception problems in computer vision, natural
language processing, and robotics: representing uncertainty, learning from data, supervised learning,
ensemble methods, unsupervised learning, structured models, learning theory, reinforcement learning. Includes
a technical project on real-world datasets.

**The rigorous ML option** — actual mathematics and actual model implementation, not library calls. The
hardest of the AI-family electives by a wide margin, with the third-lowest GPA at the 4000 level and a
double-digit withdrawal rate.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 and a statistics course
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 8/10 · Teaching C+ · Take this over CS 3804 if ML is the career rather than the tool**

courses.title: Intermediate Data Analytics and Machine Learning
courses.heading: CS 4654: Intermediate Data Analytics and Machine Learning

body.v:
Supervised and unsupervised learning strategies: regression, generalized linear models, regularization,
dimension reduction, tree-based classification methods, clustering, advanced naive Bayes, neural networks.

The practitioner's counterpart to CS 4824 — methods applied rather than derived. Good paired with it, weak as
a substitute for it.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring**
**Prerequisites:** (STAT/CMDA/CS 3654) and a statistics course

courses.title: Computer Graphics
courses.heading: CS 4204: Computer Graphics

body.v:
Hardware and software techniques for displaying graphical information: 2D and 3D geometry and
transformations, clipping and windowing, software systems, interactive graphics, shading, hidden surface
elimination, perspective depth, modeling and realism.

The real graphics course, as opposed to CS 3744. Strong if you are heading toward games, simulation,
visualization, or rendering. The sample is ten students, so the numbers carry no weight.

courses.header:
**3 credits**

courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 5/10 generally, 9/10 for graphics careers · Teaching n/d**

courses.title: Competitive Problem Solving II
courses.heading: CS 4144: Competitive Problem Solving II

body.v: No data — recently introduced.

Advanced algorithms, data structures, and implementation techniques through judged competitive programming:
advanced searching and graph algorithms, advanced dynamic programming, linear programming techniques,
computational geometry, numerical algorithms, plus optimization for efficiency.

The continuation of [CS 2144](2000-level.md#cs-2144-competitive-problem-solving-i), and the same verdict:
unusually direct technical-interview and ICPC preparation, for credit.

courses.header:

courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 6/10 generally, 8/10 for interview preparation · Teaching n/d**

courses.title: Algorithms & Society
courses.heading: CS 4014: Algorithms & Society

body.v: No data — recently introduced.

⚠️ The department's course-offerings page lists this as **"CS 4101 Algorithm and Society."** The catalog
number is **CS 4014**. Verify against the timetable before registering.

Genuinely worthwhile material with minimal technical content — and you already have CS 3604 covering adjacent
ground as a core requirement.

courses.header:

**Prerequisites:** junior standing

courses.title: Multimedia, Hypertext and Information Access
courses.heading: CS 4624: Multimedia, Hypertext and Information Access

body.v:
Architectures, concepts, data, hardware, methods, models, software, standards, structures, and technologies
for networked multimedia information systems, hypertext and hypermedia, videoconferencing, authoring and
electronic publishing, and information access — capture, representation, linking, storage, compression,
browsing, search, retrieval.

A soft capstone with a dated framing. Low risk, low technical return — but it *does* satisfy the capstone
requirement, which is worth something if your schedule is tight.

courses.header:
**3 credits · CAPSTONE-ELIGIBLE**
**Prerequisites:** see catalog

courses.title: Design of Information
courses.heading: CS 4634: Design of Information

body.v:
The higher-order properties that turn data into information: analysis of user needs, user comprehension and
local semantics, design of information organization, and design of information display appropriate to use and
setting.
Same category as CS 4624 — an easy capstone, light on engineering.

courses.header:
**3 credits · CAPSTONE-ELIGIBLE**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 and CS 3724 (C or better)

courses.title: Computer Science Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4094: Computer Science Capstone

body.v: No data — recently introduced.

Senior capstone integrating prior coursework: team-based approach to open-ended real-world problems covering
problem formulation, requirements definition, design, and implementation, with written and oral presentation
of results.
The generic default, and the most widely available option.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring, Summer**
**Prerequisites:** CS 2506 and CS 3114

courses.title: Systems & Networking Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4284: Systems & Networking Capstone

body.v:
Advanced topics in computer systems and networking: distributed and parallel processing, emerging
architectures, novel systems management and networking design, fault tolerance, robust and secure data
management. Team-based, open-ended, with design and documentation of advanced systems.
**The best capstone if you took CS 3214 and liked it.** The most technically substantial of the set.

courses.header:
**3 credits**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 and CS 3214 (C or better)

courses.title: Software Engineering Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4704: Software Engineering Capstone

body.v:
Senior project integrating software engineering knowledge: team-based problem formulation, requirements
engineering, architecture, design, implementation, integration, documentation, and delivery of a system that
solves a real-world problem.

The largest and most conventional capstone, and the highest GPA of the set. Good portfolio material, low
risk.

courses.header:

courses.title: Secure Computing Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4274: Secure Computing Capstone

body.v: Note the **corequisite** — you take this alongside CS 4264, not after it. That trips up schedules regularly.

**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 and CS 3214 · **corequisite CS 4264**

courses.title: Data-Centric Computing Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4664: Data-Centric Computing Capstone

body.v:
Project-based course on deriving insights from real-world data: team-based end-to-end projects spanning the
full data science workflow — problem statement, research questions, collection, preparation and cleaning,
iterative analysis and interpretation, synthesis into a written report and an interactive executable
codebase.
Check eligibility before planning around it.

courses.header:

**Prerequisites:** CS 3114 plus data coursework

courses.title: Human-Computer Interaction Capstone
courses.heading: CS 4784: Human-Computer Interaction Capstone

body.v:
Team-based, end-to-end, integrative interface design project drawn from departmental expertise: virtual and
augmented reality, embodied cognition, visualization, semiotic engineering, game design, personal information
management, mobile computing, design tools, educational technology, digital democracy.

courses.header:
**3 credits · Fall, Spring · usually restricted to CS majors with the HCI minor**
**Prerequisites:** CS 3724 (C or better), senior standing
courses.verdict: > **Usefulness 5/10 generally, 8/10 for product or design careers · Teaching n/d**

courses.title: Creative Computing Studio
courses.heading: CS 4644: Creative Computing Studio

body.v:
Capstone at the intersection of arts and technology: intensive immersion in game design, interactive art,
digital music, and immersive virtual reality, with teams conducting an end-to-end integrative design project.
Genuinely fun, low rigor. A legitimate choice if you have a specific portfolio piece in mind.

Team-based work on open-ended problems in computational biology and bioinformatics: algorithms for CBB,
computational models for biological systems, structure-function analysis of biomolecules, genomic data
analysis and mining, computational genomics, systems biology.

courses.title: Special Topics in Computer Science
courses.heading: CS 4894: Special Topics in Computer Science

body.v:
Advanced undergraduate topics in the design, development, use, and impact of CS solutions or software
systems. Named examples in the catalog: blockchain systems, DevOps, new programming languages, social media
software, software as a service, micro-services, end-user programming systems.

**Frequently the most current material in the department** — this is where DevOps and microservices content
actually lives, and neither has a standing course. Check what is running each term; quality tracks the
instructor rather than the course number.

courses.heading: CS 4974: Independent Study

Worth real consideration if there is a specific faculty member whose work interests you. The ratio of
learning to bureaucracy is excellent, and it is the one course you can shape entirely.

**The highest-leverage credits available to an undergraduate** if you are considering graduate school, and
strong signal for industry research roles.

Approach faculty in your junior year, not your senior spring. The students who get the most out of this
started the conversation a year before they enrolled.
